title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids
html:

A) HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY

  • 20 standard amino acids: all L (Fischer); all chiral except glycine; all S (CIP) except cysteine (R, because the CH₂SH group outranks COOH).
  • Side-chain classes: nonpolar (G A V L I M P F W), polar uncharged (S T C N Q Y), acidic (D E, −1 at pH 7.4), basic (K R H; His pKa ≈ 6 so it is mostly neutral at pH 7.4).
  • Peptide bond: amide formed by condensation (releases H₂O); planar, trans, partial double-bond character, no free rotation about C–N. Hydrolysis is favorable but slow without catalysts.
  • Structure levels: 1° sequence (covalent); 2° α-helix and β-sheet held by backbone H-bonds; 3° side-chain interactions (hydrophobic effect, salt bridges, H-bonds, disulfides); 4° multiple subunits.
  • Hydrophobic effect drives folding: burying nonpolar residues increases the entropy of water (ΔS of water > 0).
  • Proline breaks helices (no backbone N–H, rigid ring); glycine adds flexibility (common in turns).
  • Denaturation (heat, pH, urea, detergents) destroys 2°–4° structure but leaves 1° intact.
  • Enzymes lower activation energy (Ea) only; they do not change ΔG, Keq or the equilibrium position.
  • Michaelis–Menten: Km is the [S] giving ½Vmax; low Km means high apparent affinity. kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency.
  • Inhibition: competitive (raises Km, Vmax unchanged, overcome by more S); noncompetitive (lowers Vmax, Km unchanged); uncompetitive (lowers both by the same factor); mixed (lowers Vmax, Km up or down).
  • Allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal curves (cooperativity, Hill coefficient > 1), e.g. hemoglobin-like behavior.
  • Fibrous proteins (collagen: Gly-Pro-Hyp repeats, needs vitamin C) are structural; globular proteins are soluble and functional.

B) FORMULAS + PATHWAYS

FormulaMeaning and units
pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2Neutral amino acid: average the α-COOH and α-NH₃⁺ pKa values (unitless). Acidic: average the two lowest. Basic: average the two highest.
pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])Henderson–Hasselbalch; at pH = pKa the group is 50% deprotonated.
v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S])v and Vmax in M/s (or μM/s); Km and [S] in M.
1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/VmaxLineweaver–Burk: y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km, slope Km/Vmax.
Vmax = kcat[E]totalkcat (turnover number) in s⁻¹.
kcat/KmCatalytic efficiency, M⁻¹s⁻¹; diffusion limit ≈ 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.
Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki)Competitive inhibition; Ki in M.
Vmax,app = Vmax/(1 + [I]/Ki)Pure noncompetitive inhibition.

C) COMMON TRAPS + 3 MCAT-STYLE Qs

Trap 1: "L means S." L/D is the Fischer convention; R/S is CIP. Most L-amino acids are S, but L-cysteine is R. Never convert one into the other without ranking substituents.

Trap 2: "An inhibitor that raises Km lowers affinity of the enzyme." A competitive inhibitor does not change the enzyme's intrinsic affinity for substrate; it raises the apparent Km by occupying the free enzyme. Read the word "apparent".

Q1. A researcher measures an enzyme with Km = 4 μM and Vmax = 80 μM/s. A competitive inhibitor is added at [I] = 3Ki. What is the initial velocity at [S] = 4 μM?

  • A) 10 μM/s
  • B) 16 μM/s
  • C) 20 μM/s
  • D) 40 μM/s

Answer: B. Km,app = 4(1 + 3) = 16 μM. v = 80 × 4/(16 + 4) = 16 μM/s.

  • A is wrong: 10 μM/s treats the inhibitor as noncompetitive (Vmax/(1 + 3) = 20 μM/s, then halved because [S] = Km).
  • B is correct: the apparent Km is quadrupled while Vmax is unchanged.
  • C is wrong: 20 μM/s comes from multiplying Km by 3 instead of by (1 + 3), giving Km,app = 12 μM.
  • D is wrong: 40 μM/s is ½Vmax, the velocity at [S] = Km with no inhibitor present.

Q2. A protein unfolds in 8 M urea and refolds correctly when the urea is dialyzed away. Which conclusion is best supported?

  • A) Urea hydrolyzed the peptide bonds, which re-formed after dialysis.
  • B) The primary sequence contains the information needed to reach the native fold.
  • C) The protein's disulfide bonds were reduced by urea.
  • D) The native state has higher free energy than the unfolded state.

Answer: B. This is the logic of Anfinsen's experiment: the sequence alone directs folding.

  • A is wrong: urea disrupts noncovalent interactions; it does not hydrolyze peptide bonds.
  • B is correct: refolding without any other template shows sequence determines structure.
  • C is wrong: urea is not a reducing agent; β-mercaptoethanol is what reduces disulfides in that classic experiment.
  • D is wrong: spontaneous refolding means the native state is lower in free energy under physiological conditions.

Q3. At pH 7.4, which residue in a polypeptide would most likely form a salt bridge with a lysine side chain?

  • A) Glutamine
  • B) Aspartate
  • C) Histidine
  • D) Serine

Answer: B. Lysine is +1 at pH 7.4, so it pairs with a negatively charged side chain.

  • A is wrong: glutamine is an amide and stays uncharged.
  • B is correct: the aspartate side chain (pKa ≈ 3.9) is −1 at pH 7.4.
  • C is wrong: histidine (pKa ≈ 6) is mostly neutral at pH 7.4 and would be positive when charged, so it would repel lysine.
  • D is wrong: serine's hydroxyl is polar but uncharged; it can H-bond but cannot form a salt bridge.
